newsitem.title: MACAU: East Timor Nobel laureate in Macau.
newsitem.headline: East Timor Nobel laureate in Macau.

text.p: East Timor's pro-independence leader and 1996 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Jose Ramos-Horta paid tribute to the East Timorese resistance movement in exile and to the Portuguese government as he arrived in Macau.
Ramos-Horta said his Nobel prize was a "tribute to the whole resistance" against East Timor's occupation by Indonesia.

Arriving on Sunday in Portuguese-run Macau, where he was warmly feted by a crowd of exiled East Timorese, he said the prize was also a "tribute to the Portuguese government" for its support of his resistance movement.
Ramos-Horta, who shared the peace prize with East Timorese Bishop Carlos Felipe Ximenes Belo, on Sunday refrained from criticising the Philippines for barring him entry last November.
"The Philippines is the most democratic ASEAN country," he said, adding the did not want to "complicate things".
The resistance leader will give a lecture to the Foreign Correspondents' Club of nearby Hong Kong on Tuesday, before returning to Australia, his country of exile.

During his stay in Macau, Ramos-Horta is to meet Portuguese Governor General Vasco Rocha Vieira, legislature speaker Anabela Ritchie and representatives of the 200-strong East Timorese diaspora, who are mostly refugees in their twenties.
Ramos-Horta, 47, said he would thank Vieira for attending the Nobel Peace Prize awarding ceremony in Oslo last month.
The Macau government offers East Timorese refugees shelter and subsidies, allowing them to work and study in the territory.
The community consists of long-time residents of Portuguese and Chinese extraction as well as indigenous refugees in transit to Portugual or elsewhere.
Lisbon continues to demand self-determination for East Timor through a United Nations-supervised referendum on independence.
The U.N. continues to regard Portugal as the territory's rightful administering power.
Ramos-Horta is the international spokesman for the National Resistance Council, which opposes Jakarta's annexation.

East Timor's leftist FRETILIN movement, of which Ramos-Horta was foreign minister, declared the "Democratic People's Republic of East Timor" an independent country 10 days before Indonesia marched in, in 1975. Portugal has not recognised the move.
